commons:169657316.summary: Against a pale, open ground, Christ, labelled IHC XPC and followed by his disciples, stretches out his hand toward a man who holds up his withered hand as it is restored. At the left a group of men looks on, probably the scribes and Pharisees who watched to see whether Jesus would heal on the Sabbath. The miniature's clear gestures and spacious setting are typical of the narrative art of Reichenau.
facts: The Codex Egberti is a Gospel book illuminated in the scriptorium of Reichenau Abbey for Egbert of Trier (d. 993), after whom it is named.
It is still kept in Trier, in the city library (Stadtbibliothek Weberbach), as Cod. 24.
commons:169657316.notes: Folio not confirmed. Wikipedia calls Egbert bishop of Trier (980–993). The label over the left group is only partly legible in the image.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-canticle-deuter.summary: At the top the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos, blessing and holding a book, sits in a mandorla among angels as the Rock 'whose work is perfect'. Below he appears again as an avenger in a tunic, lifting his hand to heaven, grasping a 'glittering sword' and arrows and trampling those who have forsaken him, while fire and winds bring destruction. In the middle register Moses publishes the law from a hillock. The Song of Moses from Deuteronomy spreads over two pages.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
Its text is written in rustic capitals, an archaic script that once led scholars to date the manuscript to the 6th century; the drawings are now recognised as Carolingian.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-canticle-deuter.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:manuscripts2-escorial-christ-adored-.summary: In a circular glory held up by two great-winged angels sits Christ, haloed and holding a book, while below the elders and angels fall down in worship with outstretched hands: 'the four and twenty elders and the four beasts fell down and worshipped God that sat on the throne, saying, Amen; Alleluia'. The repeated bowing figures, with their huge eyes, create a powerful rhythm of adoration.
facts: The Escorial Beatus has 151 surviving leaves and 52 miniatures; it was probably made at San Millán de la Cogolla and was already in the Escorial library in the 16th century.
Its figures, with huge eyes and boldly patterned drapery, are among the most expressive in the Beatus tradition.
cur:manuscripts2-escorial-christ-adored-.notes: A similar composition appears in the San Millán Beatus (Real Academia de la Historia, Cod. 33).

princeton:21050.summary: This small, worn lead medallion shows the Baptism: at its centre stands the small nimbed figure of Christ in the Jordan, with John the Baptist reaching toward him from the left and an attendant figure, probably an angel, at the right, while rays descend from above. The reverse, still more worn, shows two nimbed figures that the museum identifies as part of an Adoration. Cheap, portable objects like this carried sacred images and stories into everyday devotion.
facts: The medallion is only 3.2 cm across and is pierced at the top, presumably so that it could be worn or attached.
Princeton catalogues it as Early Christian, dates it broadly to A.D. 500–1000, and records that it was purchased by 1937 from an unknown source.
Lead tokens and medallions bearing scenes from Christ's life are often associated with pilgrimage to the Holy Land, where the Baptism was commemorated at the Jordan.

links.label: Princeton University Art Museum object page

princeton:21050.notes: The identification of the reverse as an Adoration follows the museum's title; the surface is too worn to confirm it. Comparable lead pilgrim objects are usually dated to the 6th–7th century, but Princeton gives only the broad range, so it is kept.
